blocks.body:
The prime number theorem needs only that $\zeta(s)$ has no zeros on the line $\operatorname{Re}s=1$. To say how fast $\pi(x)/\operatorname{li}(x)\to1$, we need more: no zeros near that line. A zero-free region is a region to the left of $\operatorname{Re}s=1$ that provably contains no zeros. Its width at height $t$ translates directly into the error term in the prime number theorem.

The classical region, found by de la Vallée Poussin in 1899, has width $c/\log|t|$. Vinogradov and Korobov widened it in 1958. Every known region still shrinks to width $0$ as $|t|\to\infty$, and no one knows how to prove that $\zeta$ has no zeros in a strip $\operatorname{Re}s>1-\delta$ for any fixed $\delta>0$.

blocks.title: Why the width is the error term
blocks.body:
Use the truncated [[explicit-formula]]: for $2\le T\le x$,
$$\psi(x)-x=-\sum_{|\gamma|\le T}\frac{x^\rho}{\rho}+O\Big(\frac{x\log^2x}{T}\Big).$$
Suppose every zero with $|\gamma|\le T$ satisfies $\beta\le1-\eta(T)$. Then $|x^\rho|\le x\,e^{-\eta(T)\log x}$. The number of zeros, weighted by $1/|\rho|$, is $\ll\log^2T$ ([[nontrivial-zeros]]). So
$$|\psi(x)-x|\ll x\log^2x\;\Big(\frac1T+e^{-\eta(T)\log x}\Big).$$
Choosing $T$ to balance the two terms means making $\eta(T)\log x$ and $\log T$ about equal. A wider region (larger $\eta$) allows a larger $T$ and hence a smaller error. There is also a converse: an error term of a given shape forces a corresponding zero-free region. The simplest case, a power saving $O(x^\Theta)$ forcing $\beta\le\Theta$, is proved in [[explicit-formula]].

blocks.title: The 3–4–1 trick, made quantitative
blocks.body:
For $\sigma>1$, the logarithmic derivative of the Euler product gives
$$-\operatorname{Re}\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(\sigma+it)=\sum_n\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^\sigma}\cos(t\log n).$$
Since $3+4\cos\theta+\cos2\theta=2(1+\cos\theta)^2\ge0$ and $\Lambda(n)n^{-\sigma}\ge0$,
$$3\Big(-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(\sigma)\Big)+4\Big(-\operatorname{Re}\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(\sigma+it)\Big)+\Big(-\operatorname{Re}\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(\sigma+2it)\Big)\ge0.$$
In [[pnt]] the same inequality for $\log|\zeta|$ showed that $\zeta(1+it)\ne0$. To get a region, we feed in two bounds, valid for $1<\sigma\le2$ and $|t|\ge2$:

(A) $-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(\sigma)<\frac1{\sigma-1}+A_1$. This holds because $-\zeta'/\zeta(s)-\frac1{s-1}$ is holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $[1,2]$, hence bounded there. (Near $s=1$ it equals $-\gamma+O(s-1)$.)

(B) $-\operatorname{Re}\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(\sigma+it)<A_2\log|t|-\sum_\rho\operatorname{Re}\frac1{s-\rho}$, where $s=\sigma+it$ and every term $\operatorname{Re}\frac1{s-\rho}=\frac{\sigma-\beta}{|s-\rho|^2}$ is positive. This comes from the Hadamard product of $\xi(s)$, together with Stirling's formula for the $\Gamma$-factor. We take it as known; it is proved in Davenport's book.

The crucial feature is that (B) lets us throw away all zeros except one, since dropping positive terms only makes the right side larger.

blocks.title: de la Vallée Poussin's zero-free region (1899)
blocks.body:
There is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that $\zeta(\sigma+it)\ne0$ whenever $|t|\ge2$ and
$$\sigma > 1 - \frac{c}{\log |t|}.$$
Since there are no nontrivial zeros at all with $|t|\le2$ (the lowest has $t\approx14.13$), the region can be written for all $t$ as $\sigma>1-c'/\log(|t|+2)$.

Let $\rho=\beta+i\gamma$ be a zero with $\gamma\ge2$ (the case $\gamma\le-2$ follows by conjugation). Apply the inequality with $t=\gamma$ and $1<\sigma\le2$:

- by (A), the first term is at most $\frac3{\sigma-1}+3A_1$;
- by (B), keeping only the zero $\rho$, for which $\operatorname{Re}\frac1{\sigma+i\gamma-\rho}=\frac1{\sigma-\beta}$, the second term is at most $4A_2\log\gamma-\frac4{\sigma-\beta}$;
- by (B), dropping all zeros, the third term is at most $A_2\log(2\gamma)\le2A_2\log\gamma$.

So $0\le\frac3{\sigma-1}-\frac4{\sigma-\beta}+A\log\gamma$ with $A=6A_2+3A_1/\log2$, that is,
$$\frac4{\sigma-\beta}\le\frac3{\sigma-1}+A\log\gamma .$$
Take $\sigma=1+\delta/\log\gamma$ with $0<\delta\le\log2$, which ensures $\sigma\le2$. Then $\frac4{\sigma-\beta}\le\big(\frac3\delta+A\big)\log\gamma$, so
$$1-\beta=(\sigma-\beta)-(\sigma-1)\ \ge\ \frac{4\delta}{(3+A\delta)\log\gamma}-\frac{\delta}{\log\gamma}=\frac{\delta(1-A\delta)}{(3+A\delta)\log\gamma}.$$
With $\delta=\min(\log2,\frac1{2A})$ the numerator is at least $\delta/2$ and the denominator at most $\frac72\log\gamma$. So $1-\beta\ge\frac{\delta}{7\log\gamma}$, and $c=\delta/7$ works.

Notice where $4>3$ was used: the zero term, with coefficient $4$, beats the pole term, with coefficient $3$.

blocks.title: The classical error term
blocks.body:
There is $c>0$ such that
$$\psi(x)=x+O\big(x\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}\big)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \pi(x)=\operatorname{li}(x)+O\big(x\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}\big).$$

In the bound from the first section, take $\eta(T)=c_0/\log T$ (from the theorem) and $T=e^{\sqrt{\log x}}\le x$. Then $\eta(T)\log x=c_0\sqrt{\log x}$ and $1/T=e^{-\sqrt{\log x}}$, so
$$|\psi(x)-x|\ll x\log^2x\,e^{-\min(c_0,1)\sqrt{\log x}}\ll x\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}$$
for any $c<\min(c_0,1)$. The power of $\log x$ is absorbed by shrinking the constant. For $\pi(x)$, pass from $\psi$ to $\theta$ (an error of $O(\sqrt x)$) and use partial summation exactly as in the [[explicit-formula]] lesson.

blocks.title: Vinogradov–Korobov and the limits of the method
blocks.body:
The width $c/\log|t|$ comes from the $\log|t|$ in bound (B), which in turn reflects how large $\zeta$ can be near $\operatorname{Re}s=1$. Better bounds for $|\zeta(\sigma+it)|$ near $\sigma=1$, obtained from estimates for the exponential sums $\sum n^{-it}$ ([[exponential-sums]]), give wider regions. In 1958 Vinogradov and Korobov independently proved
$$\zeta(\sigma+it)\ne0\quad\text{for}\quad\sigma>1-\frac{c}{(\log|t|)^{2/3}(\log\log|t|)^{1/3}},\ |t|\ge3,$$
which gives $$\psi(x)=x+O\big(x\exp(-c(\log x)^{3/5}(\log\log x)^{-1/5})\big)$$. In more than sixty years the shape of this region has not been improved, apart from the constants.

A region of fixed width, with no zeros for $\sigma>1-\delta$, would give $\psi(x)=x+O(x^{1-\delta+\varepsilon})$. That is the [[quasi-rh]], and it remains open. For Dirichlet $L$-functions the same argument works with one notorious exception: it cannot exclude a single real zero very close to $1$ for a real character. Those are the [[siegel-zeros]].

blocks.title: Why the trick needs a 4 bigger than the 3
blocks.body: Try to run the argument with the simpler inequality $1+\cos\theta\ge0$. What goes wrong?
blocks.solution:
Using $1+\cos\theta\ge0$, the same steps give $\frac1{\sigma-\beta}\le\frac1{\sigma-1}+A\log\gamma$. But $\beta<1$ already implies $\frac1{\sigma-\beta}<\frac1{\sigma-1}$, so the inequality is automatically true and tells us nothing.

The general principle: the argument works with any cosine polynomial $a_0+a_1\cos\theta+\cdots+a_n\cos n\theta\ge0$ with all $a_k\ge0$ and $a_1>a_0$. The pole contributes $a_0/(\sigma-1)$ and the zero takes away $a_1/(\sigma-\beta)$. With degree $1$ this is impossible: evaluating $a_0+a_1\cos\theta$ at $\theta=\pi$ forces $a_1\le a_0$. Degree $2$ is the first that works, and $3+4\cos\theta+\cos2\theta$ is the classical choice.

blocks.title: The best ratio in degree two
blocks.body: Suppose $p(\theta)=a_0+a_1\cos\theta+a_2\cos2\theta\ge0$ for all real $\theta$. Prove that $a_1\le\sqrt2\,a_0$, and show that equality can occur.
blocks.solution:
Evaluate at $\theta=3\pi/4$, where $\cos\theta=-\frac1{\sqrt2}$ and $\cos2\theta=\cos\frac{3\pi}2=0$:
$$0\le p(3\pi/4)=a_0-\frac{a_1}{\sqrt2},$$
so $a_1\le\sqrt2a_0$. No condition on $a_2$ is needed.

For equality, take $p(\theta)=1+\sqrt2\cos\theta+\tfrac12\cos2\theta$. Using $\cos2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1$,
$$p(\theta)=\cos^2\theta+\sqrt2\cos\theta+\tfrac12=\Big(\cos\theta+\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\Big)^2\ge0 .$$
So the classical $3+4\cos\theta+\cos2\theta$, with ratio $\frac43<\sqrt2$, is not extremal. The constant $c$ in the theorem depends on the whole polynomial, not just on this ratio. Explicit versions of the zero-free region use carefully optimised polynomials of higher degree.

blocks.title: From region shape to error shape
blocks.body: Suppose there are no zeros with $\sigma>1-c/(\log|t|)^a$ for large $|t|$, where $0<a\le1$. Show that the balancing argument gives $\psi(x)-x\ll x\exp\big(-c'(\log x)^{1/(1+a)}\big)$. Check the cases $a=1$ and $a=2/3$.
blocks.solution:
Write $X=\log x$ and $L=\log T$. The error is roughly $x\big(e^{-L}+e^{-cX/L^a}\big)$, up to powers of $\log x$. The best choice of $L$ minimises the larger exponent, which happens when $L$ and $cX/L^a$ are about equal: $L^{1+a}\approx cX$, that is, $L\approx(cX)^{1/(1+a)}$. Both exponents are then of order $X^{1/(1+a)}$. (Minimising the sum $cXL^{-a}+L$ exactly gives $L=(acX)^{1/(1+a)}$, the same order.) Also $L\le X$, so $T\le x$ as required.

For $a=1$ this is $\exp(-c'\sqrt{\log x})$, de la Vallée Poussin's error. For $a=2/3$ the exponent is $(\log x)^{3/5}$; keeping track of the $\log\log$ factor gives the Vinogradov–Korobov error $(\log x)^{3/5}(\log\log x)^{-1/5}$. Each improvement in the region yields only a small gain in the exponent, which is why the error in the prime number theorem is still far from the $\sqrt x$ predicted by the Riemann hypothesis.

blocks.body:
- The bound $\sigma>1-c/\log|t|$ is stated for $|t|\ge2$; near $t=0$ write $\log(|t|+2)$. It is a region we can prove, not a description of where zeros are. All computed zeros lie on $\operatorname{Re}s=\tfrac12$.
- The 3–4–1 inequality alone proves only $\zeta(1+it)\ne0$. The region needs the quantitative input (B), whose $\log|t|$ is what limits the width.
- For a real Dirichlet character $\chi$, taking $t=0$ makes the third term involve $\chi^2=\chi_0$, which has a pole at $s=1$. That is why real zeros of real-character $L$-functions escape the argument.
- A wider region gives a better error term, but only through $\exp(-(\log x)^{\text{power}<1})$. No region of this shrinking type gives a power saving $x^{1-\delta}$.

Uniform versions of the theorem for $L(s,\chi)$, and the exceptional real zero they leave open, are the subject of [[siegel-zeros]] and lead to the [[siegel-walfisz]] theorem ([[l-functions]]). Counting how many zeros can lie in $\sigma>\tfrac12+\delta$, rather than excluding them altogether, is the theory of [[zero-density]] estimates; it often substitutes for the Riemann hypothesis. A strip of fixed width would be the [[quasi-rh]], and the full strip $\sigma>\tfrac12$ is the [[rh]]. The Vinogradov–Korobov region rests on [[exponential-sums]].

1. Show that the minimum of $3+4\cos\theta+\cos2\theta$ over $\theta$ is $0$, attained only at $\theta=\pi$ (mod $2\pi$).
2. Show that there is $c'>0$ such that $\zeta$ has no zeros with $|t|\le2$ and $\sigma\ge1-c'$. (Use that $\zeta$ has no zeros on $[\tfrac12,1)$ or on $\operatorname{Re}s=1$, and compactness.)
3. Carry out the partial summation that turns $\psi(x)=x+O(xe^{-c\sqrt{\log x}})$ into $\pi(x)=\operatorname{li}(x)+O(xe^{-c'\sqrt{\log x}})$.
4. Suppose there were a zero-free region $\sigma>1-c/\log\log|t|$ for large $|t|$. What error term would the balancing argument give for $\psi(x)-x$?
